newsitem.title: USA: Miami to stay Latam business hub despite crisis.
newsitem.headline: Miami to stay Latam business hub despite crisis.

text.p: Miami's daunting fiscal woes were expected to do little to diminish the city's role as the hub of trade and business for Latin America if the city acted quickly enough to keep things from spiraling out of control.

Miami's fiscal problems have been growing like a black cloud dimming its famed sunshine, beginning with a civic corruption scandal in September in which the city manager was arrested on bribery and corruption charges.

"In the midst of stunning successes over the past several years, here comes a bad one," Charles Jainarain, executive director of the Summit of the Americas Centre at Florida International University, said.

Since September state and local officials have uncovered a massive financial crisis, including a $68 million deficit in a city with a $275 million annual budget, and a saga of mismanagement that has prompted city residents to mount a petition drive to absorb Miami into wealthier Dade County.
But community leaders said they did not expect the fiscal crisis would alter Miami's gateway role, at least not if public officials acted quickly to address the crisis.

"If we can come up with a good solid game plan for moving forward then we can present it to people and they can develop their own comfort level," said Carol Wyllie, executive vice president of The Graham Cos real estate firm, who is chairwoman of The Beacon Council, Dade County's economic development organisation.

Wyllie noted that Miami, with a population of less than 400,000, is only a small portion of Dade County with more than 2 million people and said it is the region that has links to Latin America, not just the city.

And while other cities in Florida and elsewhere in the United States might line up to take on the Latin American gateway role if Miami stumbles, business leaders said they doubted that could happen soon, given Miami's infrastructure.

"Financing, trade finance, legal aspects of the community, already they are turned to Latin America," said Jay Malina, president of Manufacturers Export And Equity Group who also chairs a Dade County job creation panel. "With those assets, the fiscal crisis created in one of our cities doesn't really create a role. It should not, and probably will not, affect that role."
For example, executives noted that Miami International Airport handled more international air freight than any other U.S. airport last year.

On Tuesday, after intense speculation that the state would take over the city or that Miami might be forced to file for bankruptcy, Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles announced that he would not take over the city but would send advisers to help out.

The financial crisis was a sharp contrast with a run of fiscal good news that had come from Miami, a city with a thriving Hispanic community that prides itself on being the financial capital of Latin America, including hosting the massive Summit of the Americas in 1994.

"Miami is the gateway," said Jerry Haar, director of the InterAmerican Business and Labour Programme at the University of Miami's North-South Centre. "It is very much a multicultural, multilingual, hemispheric, commercial centre."

But he said of the budget scandal, "Isn't it ironic that we point our finger at the inefficiency, corruption and moral decay that still runs rampant in Latin America? The thing is, we've got to clean up our own backyard."
